A company's business assets are assumed to equal its annual sales: one dollar of plant and equipment produces one dollar of sales a year. So the number that really matters is return on capital, or ROC - your profit as a percent of those assets, which is essentially your profit margin. Push it up and the stock, your salary, and your bonus all climb with it. Click Continue.
What actually makes a company profitable

Still on the Financials tab, find R&D / Ad Spend in the Operations panel and click its Adjust button. Spending more here raises long-term profitability but dents short-term earnings: short-term pain for long-term gain. Take the chair

A bank earns on the spread: it pays little or nothing on the deposits it holds, then lends that money out (corporate, consumer, and mortgage loans) and buys bonds at higher yields. A wider spread and a healthy loan book mean profit; a downturn that wrecks the loan book is what sinks a bank. Click Continue.
How a bank makes money

Open the Financials tab. Notice there's no growth-rate or R&D knob like an industrial company - instead you get a Banking panel showing your loan portfolio, deposits, and line of credit. Banks mostly run themselves; your job is to set the strategy. Click Continue.
A bank is steered differently

Your asset allocation IS the bank's strategy, and every choice trades yield against risk. From safest to riskiest: Cash equivalents (cash + T-bills) earn the least but keep the bank liquid - you must hold at least 10% as a downturn buffer. Bonds pay a steady coupon, but their value moves opposite to interest rates, so they're a bargain when rates are high. Prime mortgages are solid, low-default home loans. Consumer loans pay more but default more in a recession. Subprime mortgages pay the most and are the most dangerous: in a credit crisis like 2008 they collapse and freeze, and you cannot sell without a huge loss. Two screens guide you - Interest Rates (favor bonds when rates are high) and Economic Data (chase yield with consumer and subprime in a boom; retreat to prime, bonds, and cash when a recession looms). Click Continue.

Open the Banking dropdown and click Set Allocation. For a steady starter bank in normal times, try roughly 30% prime mortgages, 20% consumer loans, 30% bonds, 0% subprime, and 20% cash (it must total 100%, with at least 10% cash). Once you read the cycle you can get aggressive: pile into subprime in a strong economy, or load up on bonds when interest rates spike. Apply your mix, then click Continue.
Set your mix
